text: A bank statement is a list of lines, and reading one is easy to get slightly wrong.
Miss one line, or read one number wrong, and the ledger is off for good.
So Summa doesn't trust what it reads until the statement proves it.
Every statement prints an opening balance and a closing balance.
Summa starts from the opening balance and adds every line it read.
If the total lands exactly on the closing balance, the statement is trusted.
If it's off by even one unit, the whole statement is rejected.
Two exports from the same account can overlap, and the first one can stop halfway through a day.
Cut by date, and you either count that day twice or lose the rest of it.
So Summa finds the line where the first export's running balance stopped, and cuts right after it.
Nothing is counted twice, and nothing is lost.
Every statement line in the ledger came from a statement that added up.
